answers.question: Is shade-grown coffee under trees counted as forest?
answers.answer:
Generally, no. Under the EUDR definition, an “agricultural plantation” includes agroforestry systems “where crops are grown under tree cover,” and agricultural plantations are excluded from “forest.” [EUDR Art. 2(6)] Shade-grown coffee under trees would therefore generally fall outside the forest definition if it is an agricultural production system or agroforestry system [EUDR Art. 2(6)]. The Commission guidance likewise describes agroforestry as crops and trees growing together and states that such systems are agricultural use rather than forests [EC Guidance §11.4(d) (part 1)].

However, the passages do not establish that every shade-grown coffee site automatically qualifies: the relevant facts—such as whether it is an agricultural production system—remain to be assessed. A forest replaced by an agricultural plantation may still constitute deforestation under the Regulation [EC FAQ Q4.14]. A forest-map overlap alone does not determine the legal classification [Note: JRC GFC2020 forest map and coffee].

answers.question: What is the legal definition of forest?
answers.answer: Under the EUDR, “forest” means land spanning more than 0.5 hectares with trees higher than 5 metres and canopy cover exceeding 10%, or with trees able to reach those thresholds in situ. Land predominantly under agricultural or urban use is excluded [EUDR Art. 2(4)].

answers.question: What does deforestation mean in this regulation?
answers.answer:
In the EUDR, “deforestation” means “the conversion of forest to agricultural use, whether human-induced or not.” [EUDR Art. 2(3)] The definition therefore covers conversion caused by natural events as well as by people [EC FAQ Q4.12]. For example, forest affected by fire and subsequently converted into agricultural land is deforestation; if it is allowed to regenerate, it is not [EC FAQ Q4.12].

The conversion’s extent, legal registration, plot boundaries, or who or what caused it do not determine whether it is deforestation [EC Guidance §11.2 (part 1)]. However, conversion of forest to a land use that is not agricultural use does not fall within this definition [EC Guidance §11.2 (part 1)].

answers.question: What is the cut-off date for deforestation-free products?
answers.answer: The cut-off date is 31 December 2020. Products are “deforestation-free” only if the relevant commodities were produced on land not subject to deforestation after that date. For wood-containing products, the wood must also have been harvested without inducing forest degradation after 31 December 2020 [EUDR Art. 2(13)]. The Commission’s guidance confirms that compliance checks look back to determine whether the cropland was previously forest since this cut-off date [EC FAQ Q5.12]. The rule therefore leaves open the factual assessment of whether deforestation or forest degradation occurred after 31 December 2020 [EUDR Art. 2(13)].

answers.question: What is forest degradation?
answers.answer:
“Forest degradation” means structural changes to forest cover involving conversion of:  

- primary forests or naturally regenerating forests into plantation forests or other wooded land; or  
- primary forests into planted forests [EUDR Art. 2(7)].

For wood products, the relevant question is whether harvesting activities after 31 December 2020 caused or may cause such a conversion, including through planned post-harvesting activities [EC FAQ Q4.6 (part 1)]. The harvesting must have a causal role: degradation caused by climate change, disease, or fires is outside this specific scope [EC FAQ Q4.5 (part 1)]. If a degraded forest later regenerates into a category not covered by the definition, future wood harvesting may be considered deforestation-free; if its degraded status persists, it may not be [EC FAQ Q4.5 (part 2)].

answers.question: When is a polygon needed for the geolocation of a plot?
answers.answer:
A polygon is needed when the plot is more than four hectares and is used to produce relevant commodities other than cattle. The polygon must contain sufficient latitude and longitude points to describe the plot’s perimeter [EUDR Art. 2(28)].

For plots below four hectares, one latitude-and-longitude point may be used instead [EC FAQ Q1.8]. For cattle, polygons are not required; single geolocation points are required for the relevant establishments [EC FAQ Q1.8]. A circumference around a central point is not an alternative to a polygon [EC FAQ Q1.16].

For micro or small primary operators, the specified geolocation may instead be replaced by the postal address of all plots or the relevant establishment, under the stated simplified regime [EUDR Art. 4a(5)].

answers.question: From what date does the EUDR apply?
answers.answer: The EUDR generally applies from 30 December 2026 for Articles 3–13, 16–24, 26, 31 and 32 [EUDR Art. 38(2)]. However, for operators that are natural persons or micro- or small undertakings established as such by 31 December 2024, those provisions apply from 30 June 2027, except for products covered by the Annex to Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 [EUDR Art. 38(3)]. The Regulation itself entered into force on the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal [EUDR Art. 38(1)]. Products produced before the date indicated in Article 38(1) are generally outside its scope, subject to Article 37(3) [EUDR Art. 1(2)].

answers.question: When does the regulation apply to micro and small undertakings?
answers.answer: For micro- or small undertakings established as such by 31 December 2024, the EUDR applies from 30 June 2027, except for products covered by the Annex to Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 [EUDR Art. 38(3)]. This applies irrespective of legal form and includes natural persons [EUDR Art. 38(3)]. The relevant classification is under Article 3(1) or Article 3(2), first subparagraph, of Directive 2013/34/EU [EUDR Art. 38(3)][EUDR Art. 2(30)]. The Commission states that the decisive issue is whether the operator had that status on 31 December 2024, using the thresholds then in force; group thresholds and the 2003 Commission recommendation are not relevant [EC FAQ Q3.10]. Separately, micro or small primary operators are exempt from specified obligations under Article 4a(1) [EUDR Art. 4a(1)].

answers.question: What information and geolocation must operators collect?
answers.answer:
Operators must collect, organise and retain for five years information, documents and data demonstrating compliance, with evidence, for each relevant product. This includes: a product description (including trade name, type, relevant commodities/products, and—where wood is involved—the species’ common and full scientific names); quantity; country of production and, where relevant, its parts; and the geolocation of all plots of land where the commodities were produced, together with the production date or time range [EUDR Art. 9(1)].

For micro or small primary operators, the plot geolocation may be replaced by the postal address of all plots or of the establishment from which the commodities were produced [EUDR Art. 4a(5)]. The address must clearly correspond to the relevant geographic location, and the operator may choose between geolocation and postal address [Reg. 2025/2650 Recital 9]. Operators must submit the geolocation information; national prohibitions on sharing it do not remove that obligation [EC FAQ Q1.31].

answers.question: Can competent authorities use satellite imagery in their checks?
answers.answer: Yes. Competent authorities may use satellite imagery as part of their checks. The EUDR expressly permits “technical and scientific means” adequate to determine whether products are deforestation-free, including Earth observation data from Copernicus and other publicly or privately available sources [EUDR Art. 18(2)]. Commission guidance also states that spatial imagery tools can help competent authorities perform checks, but the Regulation does not require a specific tool or minimum imagery resolution [EC FAQ Q5.18]. Authorities may cross-check operators’ geolocation coordinates against satellite images or forest-cover maps when assessing compliance with the deforestation-free requirement [EC FAQ Q1.19]. The passages do not specify a mandatory imagery provider, resolution threshold, or single methodology [EC FAQ Q5.18].

answers.question: Does tree loss in the Hansen dataset prove deforestation?
answers.answer: No. Hansen GFC records the year a 30 m pixel “lost tree canopy,” but loss can result from “clearing, pruning, storms, fire or plantation harvest.” It “does not say whether land was converted to agricultural use,” which the dataset note identifies as what the EUDR definition of deforestation requires [Note: Hansen Global Forest Change loss is not deforestation]. The Commission describes deforestation under Article 2 EUDR as “the conversion of forest to agricultural use, whether human-induced or not.” [EC FAQ Q4.1] Thus, Hansen tree loss does not prove EUDR deforestation. The passages leave open whether any particular loss event involved conversion of forest to agricultural use [Note: Hansen Global Forest Change loss is not deforestation][EC FAQ Q4.1].

answers.question: Does the EUDR agricultural-use exclusion mean coffee cultivated under shade trees is not forest?
answers.answer: No. Shade trees do not automatically mean that coffee-growing land is “forest.” The EUDR definition excludes land “predominantly under agricultural … land use” [EUDR Art. 2(4)]. Commission guidance states that agricultural plantations include “agroforestry systems where crops are grown under tree cover,” and that such plantations are agricultural use and excluded from “forest” [EC Guidance §11.4(c)]. Thus, coffee cultivated under shade trees may fall outside the forest definition where it qualifies as an agricultural plantation or the predominant land use is agriculture. However, the passages do not establish that every shade-coffee plot qualifies: the relevant facts include whether the land is an agroforestry system or otherwise predominantly agricultural. Small-scale production of side products or occasional grazing in forests does not, by itself, make agricultural use predominant [EC Guidance §11.4(b) (part 1)][EC Guidance §11.4(b) (part 2)].

answers.question: Does tree-cover loss within an existing coffee plantation constitute deforestation under the EUDR?
answers.answer:
Not necessarily. Under Article 2(6), an agricultural plantation includes land with tree stands in agricultural production systems and “all plantations of relevant commodities other than wood”; agricultural plantations are excluded from “forest.” [EUDR Art. 2(6)] Coffee plantations therefore generally fall within agricultural use and outside the EUDR forest definition [EC FAQ Q9.10.1 (part 1)] [EC Guidance §11.4(c)].

Accordingly, loss of tree cover within an existing coffee plantation does not, on these passages alone, constitute EUDR deforestation merely because canopy was lost. The EUDR-relevant question is whether forest was converted to agricultural use; a loss dataset may record clearing, pruning, storms, fire, or harvest and does not establish such conversion [Note: Hansen Global Forest Change loss is not deforestation]. The passages leave open the classification of the particular land before the loss and whether the plantation meets the agricultural-plantation criteria.

answers.question: Does forest degradation after 31 December 2020 make coffee non-compliant, or does that rule apply only to wood?
answers.answer:
Forest degradation after 31 December 2020 does not, on the wording provided, independently make coffee non-compliant. Article 2(13)(a) defines “deforestation-free” for relevant commodities generally—including coffee—as production on land not subject to deforestation after that date. The separate forest-degradation condition in Article 2(13)(b) applies “in the case of relevant products that contain or have been made using wood.” [EUDR Art. 2(13)]

Thus, coffee must satisfy the applicable deforestation-free criterion, along with other EUDR requirements; the passages do not extend the forest-degradation limb to coffee. The Commission guidance confirms that the special two-criterion treatment concerns wood [EC FAQ Q4.3]. Coffee is listed as a relevant commodity, but that recital does not alter Article 2(13)’s distinction [Reg. 2025/2650 Recital 1].

answers.question: If a forest is damaged by fire or a storm and then regrows, is that deforestation?
answers.answer: No. Fire or storm damage followed by natural regeneration is not, by itself, “deforestation.” The EUDR defines deforestation as conversion of forest to agricultural use, whether human-induced or not [EUDR Art. 2(3)]. The Commission explains that a fire followed by conversion to agricultural land is deforestation, but “if the affected forest is allowed to regenerate,” it is not deforestation, and wood may be sourced once it has regrown [EC FAQ Q4.12]. It also states that fire-related forest degradation unrelated to harvesting does not prevent products from being considered deforestation-free, provided harvesting did not induce the degradation and sufficient evidence supports that conclusion [EC FAQ Q4.7]. The passages do not specify every evidentiary requirement for proving regeneration or causation.

answers.question: How can the geolocation of a plot be checked against satellite images or forest cover maps?
answers.answer: Geolocation can be checked by comparing the plot’s coordinates with satellite imagery, forest-cover maps, or other Earth-observation data to assess whether the product is deforestation-free [EUDR Art. 18(2)] [EC FAQ Q1.19]. The operator must collect coordinates for all plots contributing to the product; if it cannot, the product should not be placed on the EU market or exported [EC FAQ Q1.19]. The EUDR Information System allows users to enter, adjust, and visualise coordinates, but it is not an advanced GIS tool and does not provide background satellite imagery [EC FAQ Q7.5]. Users may therefore verify coordinates using other tools, including free online map services [EC FAQ Q7.5]. Forest-cover maps are evidence for cross-checking, not necessarily conclusive: the JRC map note reports limitations and says forest overlap alone does not establish non-compliance [Note: JRC GFC2020 forest map and coffee].

answers.question: What counts as a plot of land when a coffee estate has several parts?
answers.answer: A “plot of land” is land within one real-estate property recognised under the law of the country of production, with sufficiently homogeneous conditions to assess the aggregate deforestation and forest-degradation risk [EUDR Art. 2(27)]. Thus, a coffee estate may count as one plot if the entire property is sufficiently homogeneous; otherwise, only a distinct part may qualify [EC FAQ Q1.15 (part 1)]. You need identify the plot(s) actually used to produce coffee intended for the EU market, not every plot owned by the estate [EC FAQ Q4.2]. If several qualifying plots supply the coffee, they may be included in one due-diligence statement, but each plot requires its own polygon; one polygon cannot cover several plots [EC FAQ Q1.14]. The passages leave open how national property law and “sufficiently homogeneous” conditions apply to the particular estate.

answers.question: What does the EUDR require when a coffee plot is located in a designated reserve forest or protected area?
answers.answer: The EUDR requires coffee placed on the EU market or exported to have been produced on a designated “plot of land”; lack of a land registry or formal title does not prevent designation where land is de facto used as a plot [EC FAQ Q1.6]. Indian law defines a “reserved forest” as land settled and notified under Chapter II, and a “protected forest” as government-disposed land placed under special protection or declared protected under the specified provisions [Karnataka Forest Act s.2 (part 4)]. These passages do not state that coffee from a reserve forest or protected area is automatically prohibited, nor do they specify any additional EUDR requirement solely because of that designation.

answers.question: Is clearing land or forming a plantation allowed inside a reserved forest in Karnataka?
answers.answer:
No. Under the Karnataka Forest Act, in a reserved forest, a person who “clears or breaks up any land for cultivation or any other purpose” commits a prohibited act [Karnataka Forest Act s.24 (part 1)]. Forming a plantation would ordinarily involve clearing or breaking up land for cultivation, so it is covered by that prohibition to the extent the activity involves such clearing [Karnataka Forest Act s.24 (part 1)].

The passages do not state whether any specific permission, lease, or statutory exception could authorize plantation activity. They do show that the forest ceases to be reserved only from a date specified in a State Government notification, subject generally to a resolution by both Houses of the State Legislature [Karnataka Forest Act s.28]. Thus, the passages do not establish that clearing or plantation is allowed while the land remains a reserved forest.

answers.question: Is rubber grown under trees treated as agricultural use or as forest?
answers.answer:
Rubber grown under trees is treated as agricultural use, not forest, where it falls within an agricultural plantation or agroforestry system. The EUDR defines an agricultural plantation to include “agroforestry systems where crops are grown under tree cover” and states that agricultural plantations are excluded from “forest” [EUDR Art. 2(6)]. Commission guidance specifically confirms that rubber cultivation falls within this definition, including areas with rubber trees [EC FAQ Q4.14][EC Guidance §11.4(c)]. The Recital likewise says agroforestry systems with crops under tree cover constitute agricultural use rather than forest [EUDR Recital 37].

However, replacing an existing forest with a rubber plantation is considered deforestation under the Regulation [EC FAQ Q4.14].

answers.question: How can farmers give the location of their plots when land titles or property registers are missing?
answers.answer: Farmers can provide the geolocation of their plots even if the plots are not recorded in a land registry and they lack land IDs or titles. The required information is the plot’s latitude and longitude, using at least six decimal digits; plots over four hectares generally require a polygon describing the perimeter [EUDR Art. 2(28)]. The Commission states that no personal information from farmers is required unless they are direct suppliers or operators; the plot’s geolocation is sufficient [EC FAQ Q1.10 (part 1)]. If domestic law does not require a land title to produce and commercialise agricultural products, the EUDR does not impose that requirement, although operators must verify compliance with applicable national laws [EC FAQ Q1.10 (part 1)]. Micro or small primary operators may instead provide the postal address of each plot or the producing establishment, where it corresponds to the geographic location [EUDR Art. 4a(5)][Reg. 2025/2650 Recital 9].

answers.question: Can one polygon be drawn around several separate coffee plots?
answers.answer: No. Each polygon should describe the perimeter of one single plot of land, whether contiguous or not [EC FAQ Q1.14]. A polygon cannot instead enclose a broader area containing plots only in some parts [EC FAQ Q1.14]. For plots larger than four hectares, the EUDR requires sufficient latitude and longitude points to describe the perimeter of each plot [EUDR Art. 2(28)].

answers.question: Can a small coffee grower give a postal address instead of GPS coordinates?
answers.answer: Yes—if the grower qualifies as a micro or small primary operator, the geolocation may be replaced by the postal address of all relevant plots or of the establishment where the coffee was produced [EUDR Art. 4a(5)]. This is an alternative, not an additional requirement: the operator may choose between geolocation and the qualifying postal address [Reg. 2025/2650 Recital 9]. The passages do not specify further criteria for determining whether a particular grower qualifies as “micro or small.”

answers.question: What is the difference between forest and other wooded land in the regulation?
answers.answer:
“Forest” is the Regulation’s primary category, based on the FAO definition [EC FAQ Q4.13]. “Other wooded land” is defined residually as land “not classified as ‘forest’” that exceeds 0.5 hectares and has either trees over 5 metres with 5–10% canopy cover, trees capable of reaching those thresholds in situ, or combined shrub, bush and tree cover above 10%; predominantly agricultural or urban land is excluded [EUDR Art. 2(12)].

Thus, the key difference is that other wooded land falls outside the forest classification but meets specified size, vegetation and cover thresholds [EUDR Art. 2(12)]. The Regulation treats conversion of primary or naturally regenerating forest into other wooded land as forest degradation [EC FAQ Q4.13][EC FAQ Q4.4]. The passages do not provide the full FAO forest definition or resolve every borderline classification.

answers.question: What does primary forest mean?
answers.answer:
“Primary forest” means a naturally regenerated forest of native tree species where:

- there are no clearly visible indications of human activities; and
- ecological processes are not significantly disturbed [EUDR Art. 2(8)].

The passage does not further define “naturally regenerated,” “clearly visible indications,” or “significantly disturbed.”

answers.question: What fines and other penalties can be imposed for breaking the regulation?
answers.answer:
Member States must establish and implement penalties for EUDR infringements [EUDR Art. 25(1)]. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive [EUDR Art. 25(2)]. They may include:

- fines proportionate to environmental damage and the value of the commodities/products, designed to remove economic benefits and increased for repeat infringements; for legal persons, the maximum fine must be at least 4% of the relevant preceding financial year’s total EU-wide turnover, and may need to exceed the economic benefit gained; [EUDR Art. 25(2)]
- confiscation of products and infringement-related revenues; [EUDR Art. 25(2)]
- exclusion for up to 12 months from public procurement and public funding; [EUDR Art. 25(2)]
- temporary prohibition on placing/making products available on the market or exporting them for serious or repeated infringements; and [EUDR Art. 25(2)]
- prohibition on using simplified due diligence for serious or repeated infringements [EUDR Art. 25(2)].

Member States define the detailed penalties and fine levels [EC FAQ Q10.2]. Final judgments against legal persons and penalties imposed must be notified and published by the Commission [EUDR Art. 25(3)].

answers.question: Who can declare land to be a reserved forest in Karnataka?
answers.answer: The State Government can declare land to be a reserved forest in Karnataka. It may constitute as a reserved forest government-owned land, land over which it has proprietary rights, or forest produce to which it is entitled, following the procedure in the Act [Karnataka Forest Act s.3]. After claims, appeals, and required proceedings have been completed, the State Government must publish a notification clearly specifying the forest’s boundaries and declaring it a reserved forest from the date stated in the notification [Karnataka Forest Act s.17]. A “reserved forest” is land settled and notified under Chapter II of the Karnataka Forest Act [Karnataka Forest Act s.2 (part 4)].

answers.question: Is forest cleared to build a road after 2020 counted as deforestation?
answers.answer:
No, not under the EUDR’s definition of deforestation. Article 2(3), as quoted in Commission guidance, defines deforestation as “conversion of forest to agricultural use.” The guidance states that conversion for “urban development or infrastructure does not fall under the deforestation definition” and gives as an example wood from a forest area “legally harvested to build a road.” [EC FAQ Q4.11]

The EUDR’s “deforestation-free” definition nevertheless requires production on land “that has not been subject to deforestation after 31 December, 2020.” [EUDR Art. 2(13)] The passages therefore leave open requirements or consequences not specifically addressed here, including how other rules apply to the particular road project.

answers.question: What happens to commodities grown on communal or public land that is not real estate?
answers.answer: Commodities grown on public or communal land that is not real estate may still be placed on the EU market or exported if the land can be designated as a “plot of land.” [EC FAQ Q1.6] A plot of land is land within a single real-estate property recognised under the production country’s law, with sufficiently homogeneous conditions for assessing deforestation and forest-degradation risk [EUDR Art. 2(27)]. However, the absence of a land registry or formal title should not by itself prevent designation where the land is de facto used as a plot of land [EC FAQ Q1.6]. The passages do not specify further requirements for communal or public ownership.
